title: Involuntary churn: when a failed payment costs you a customer
description: Understand involuntary SaaS churn, separate it from cancellations, and build a practical workflow for recovering failed subscription payments.
answer: Involuntary churn is customer loss caused by a payment or billing failure rather than a deliberate cancellation. A customer who still wants your product can become unpaid because their subscription charge did not complete.

sections.title: A billing failure is a different problem from a cancellation
sections.body:
A customer who cancels because the product is not useful needs a different response from a customer whose card was declined. If both disappear into one churn number, your team loses the ability to diagnose either problem.

Start by separating voluntary cancellations from payment-related losses. Then track the failed invoice, the remaining balance, the customer’s saved payment methods, and the eventual outcome. A failed attempt is an event; a lost customer is an outcome. They are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Where delinquent churn fits
sections.body:
You may also see teams call this delinquent churn or payment-related churn. Define the label before reporting it: a delinquent account has an overdue payment, but it may still recover before the customer is lost. Treating every overdue account as churn immediately can overstate the problem.

Track a progression from failed payment to overdue invoice, then to recovery or unresolved customer loss. That gives your finance and customer teams the same operational view without treating the first decline as the end of the relationship.

sections.title: Measure the customer and the money separately
sections.body:
For customer churn, divide customers lost through billing failures during a period by customers at the start of that period. For revenue exposure, add the outstanding recurring invoice balances you are trying to recover. Keep the time period and population consistent.

Do not count every failed card attempt as a separate customer or a new invoice. If one invoice has four unsuccessful attempts, it is still one debt. Likewise, an invoice that eventually gets paid belongs in failure history but should no longer count as unpaid revenue.

Our recovery opportunity calculator models a simple scenario from your own assumptions. It does not predict recovery performance or customer lifetime value.

sections.title: Build a recovery workflow around the actual invoice
sections.body:
1. Find subscription payment failures in a clear date range.
  2. Check whether each original invoice still has an unpaid balance.
  3. Review the saved cards and their eligibility for another attempt.
  4. Start a controlled recovery run and stop for each invoice when it is paid.
  5. Separate payments collected from unresolved failures and outcomes that need review.

This workflow makes recovery accountable. It also avoids inflating results by calling an already-paid invoice a new recovery.

sections.title: Use communication when a charge alone cannot solve it
sections.body:
Some failures need a new card, customer authentication, or a conversation about the account. More retries are not a substitute for those actions. Keep your customer-facing billing messages clear: what failed, what remains due, and how to update the payment method.

Rebound focuses on a specific part of this process: an operator starts a run against eligible unpaid subscription invoices, and the tool tries eligible saved cards in sequence. It does not claim to eliminate every source of churn.

sections.title: A weekly review that keeps the distinction visible
sections.body:
Use one short review for the customers whose billing issues remain unresolved. Keep the original invoice reference, next action, owner, and planned follow-up date. Review confirmed payments separately from cases that are simply waiting for the next retry.

At the reporting cutoff, classify customers using your documented loss definition. Keep later recoveries visible instead of presenting them as newly acquired customers. The delinquent churn example shows how an overdue population can produce a smaller actual churn count.

When the next action is unclear, begin with the failed-payment reconciliation checklist. A clean invoice list is more useful than changing a retention policy in response to an inflated failure count.

title: How to review and recover failed Stripe subscription payments
description: A practical guide to reviewing failed Stripe payments, matching them to unpaid invoices, checking saved cards, and tracing recovery outcomes.
answer: Start with failed subscription payment attempts, then check the current status and balance of the original invoice. Use eligible saved cards to retry unpaid invoices, and confirm the outcome against the invoice and payment records.

sections.title: Start with a date range you can explain
sections.body:
Decide whether you are asking which payments failed during a period or which invoices remain unpaid today. These are different views. An invoice can fail in one month and be paid in another; an old failure can remain visible even after its debt is resolved.

Use one timezone consistently. Rebound’s collection filters use New York calendar dates, and the app starts with the last 15 days including today. The list loads automatically, so changing the dates is optional.

sections.title: Read failures without multiplying the debt
sections.body:
Review the customer, the invoice reference, the amount still due, and the saved cards. Multiple failed attempts can belong to the same invoice. Group those attempts before calculating the total you intend to collect.

The reason attached to a failed attempt tells you what happened at that moment. The invoice’s current state tells you whether there is still a balance to collect. Keep both pieces of information visible.

sections.title: Check which invoice states are payable
sections.body:
Do not treat every failed payment record as permission to collect. Some invoices are already paid or voided. Others may have an unresolved payment outcome that needs attention before another attempt.

A written-off invoice is not the same as a voided invoice. Stripe documents a payment transition for uncollectible invoices; voided invoices are cancelled. Rebound includes written-off subscription invoices in manual recovery when otherwise eligible, while keeping voided invoices excluded. See our invoice status guide.

sections.title: Run recovery and verify the result
sections.body:
In Rebound, review the loaded list and click Start recovery to begin real collection attempts. Each eligible saved physical card is tried at most once per invoice in that run. The tool stops trying that invoice when it is paid, when the eligible cards are exhausted, or when an uncertain outcome needs review.

After a run, inspect the invoice-level result and card-attempt history. A successful outcome should link back to the original Stripe invoice. Keep a record of the amount collected, which invoice was paid, and when the result was confirmed.

Coordinate this process with any retry policy you already run in Stripe or another tool. Looking at a failure list should never itself trigger a charge.

sections.title: Reconcile the selection before evaluating success
sections.body:
Keep the selected date range, matched invoice IDs, and balances at the start of the run. Compare that fixed population with confirmed results afterward. If you change dates midway through the review, label the new population rather than treating it as the same experiment.

Report why visible invoices are excluded from collection. Already-paid history, cancelled invoices, missing eligible cards, and unresolved payment states are different conditions. A smaller actionable queue is not proof that the failure scan missed records.

For the complete count check, use the Stripe reporting guide. For confirming where a successful payment originated, follow the attribution checklist rather than relying on timing alone.

seoTitle: How to recover failed Stripe subscription payments

title: Dunning, payment retries, and saved-card fallback: what’s the difference?
description: Learn how dunning messages, timed payment retries, and saved-card fallback address different parts of subscription revenue recovery.
answer: Dunning is the broader process of following up on overdue payments. Timed retries decide when to attempt collection again. Saved-card fallback tries another eligible card when an attempt fails. These solve different parts of a billing failure.

sections.title: Dunning is the recovery conversation
sections.body:
A useful dunning process tells a customer that something went wrong and gives them a way to resolve it. That might mean updating a card, completing authentication, or clarifying an invoice. The message should identify the problem without assuming the customer wanted to cancel.

The operational side matters too: decide who reviews unresolved accounts, when access changes, and how your team records the outcome. Sending emails without checking whether the invoice has since been paid creates a confusing customer experience.

sections.title: Timed retries answer when to try again
sections.body:
A temporary failure can resolve later, so another attempt at a different time may help. Stripe’s Smart Retries is a timing-based recovery feature. Stripe also documents a payment-method priority order for subscription retries.

Updating the customer default is not always the same as updating the subscription default. Check which payment method your billing configuration actually uses. Read the current Stripe retry documentation before changing a policy.

sections.title: Card fallback answers which saved card to try
sections.body:
Consider an unpaid subscription invoice for $96. The customer has three saved cards. The first attempt fails. A fallback workflow can move to another eligible card instead of requiring an operator to open the account and repeat the same steps by hand.

Rebound uses a manual-start workflow: choose a date range, review the unpaid invoices, and start recovery. It tries eligible saved cards once each per invoice in that run and stops when payment succeeds. This example describes the workflow, not a promise that the second card will work.

sections.title: Choose the response that matches the failure
sections.body:
• A temporary funding problem: review the timing and retry policy.
  • A different eligible card is already saved: consider a controlled fallback attempt.
  • Authentication or a new method is required: involve the customer.
  • The result of a charge is unknown: verify the outcome before attempting another payment.

Use the original invoice as the shared reference across these actions. That makes it easier to coordinate tools and distinguish one debt from its many attempts.

sections.title: Assign one owner to the collection journey
sections.body:
If several systems can charge and send messages, map their responsibilities around the same invoice. One team should be able to say which attempt is pending, which communication was sent, and what evidence will close the case.

A simple handoff rule helps: an uncertain payment waits for verification; a case requiring customer input receives an appropriate message; a confirmed paid invoice stops collection follow-up. That rule is more useful than increasing every retry count.

Use the customer email templates for communication and the timing-versus-fallback comparison when reviewing which part of recovery a tool actually handles.

title: Uncollectible vs. void Stripe invoices: can you still recover the payment?
description: Understand the difference between written-off and voided Stripe invoices, and what each state means for a subscription recovery workflow.
answer: Uncollectible means an invoice has been written off, and Stripe supports paying that original invoice. Void means the invoice has been cancelled. A recovery workflow must distinguish these states rather than treating both as an ordinary failed charge.

sections.title: A failure reason and an invoice status tell different stories
sections.body:
A card decline describes an unsuccessful attempt to collect. An invoice status describes the invoice itself. Looking back at a year of failures, you may see a decline attached to an invoice that is now paid, written off, or voided.

This is why a date-filtered failure report and a list of invoices you can collect today can contain different totals. Always check the current remaining balance as well as the original failure.

sections.title: Uncollectible invoices can still be paid
sections.body:
An uncollectible invoice represents debt that was written off. Stripe’s documented workflow includes a transition from uncollectible to paid when payment succeeds. If an attempt fails, it remains uncollectible.

In Rebound, the written-off status alone does not exclude a subscription invoice from a manual run. The invoice must still pass the other eligibility checks. Its remaining balance and payment outcome are checked before a collection attempt.

This allows you to review older unpaid subscription debt without creating a new, unrelated charge simply to reproduce the invoice amount.

sections.title: A voided invoice is cancelled
sections.body:
A voided invoice should not be treated as active debt in the retry list. Rebound keeps it visible where it is part of failure history, but does not include it in a recovery run.

If the invoice was cancelled incorrectly or the amount needs changing, review the billing record in Stripe and decide what the correct invoice should be. Do not use a retry tool to bypass an invoice cancellation.

sections.title: Use a clear review checklist
sections.body:
1. Find the original invoice and verify the customer and subscription.
  2. Check the current invoice status and remaining amount.
  3. Check whether a payment is still processing or its result is uncertain.
  4. Review the saved cards and their eligibility.
  5. Start collection only for the intended invoices and keep the resulting Stripe references.

Rebound’s list separates invoice history from inclusion in a recovery run. A row being visible does not mean a charge is happening, and opening the list does not start collection.

sections.title: Keep write-offs, recoveries, and reporting separate
sections.body:
Recovering written-off debt can be a useful cash outcome without proving that the customer has returned. Record the invoice payment and inspect subscription status separately. Do not automatically add the invoice amount to new MRR or expansion revenue.

If finance deliberately forgave an amount or ended the commercial relationship, resolve that business decision before putting historical invoices into a collection run. Technical payability alone is not the whole collection policy.

After a payment, retain the original invoice reference and the confirmed collected amount. The measurement guide explains the difference between cash recovery and retained recurring revenue; the subscription status guide explains why an invoice result is not the entire account state.

sources: Stripe: invoice transitions and payment endpoints

title: Delinquent churn: how to find, measure, and reduce it
description: Separate overdue accounts from lost customers. Use a clear delinquent churn definition, a worked example, and a practical subscription recovery checklist.
answer: Delinquent churn is customer loss following an unresolved overdue subscription payment. An overdue invoice is a recovery opportunity; it becomes churn only when the customer meets your defined loss criteria.

sections.title: Do not call every late payment churn
sections.body:
A subscription payment fails on Monday. The customer pays on Wednesday and keeps using the product. That was a billing incident, not a lost customer. If Monday’s dashboard calls it churn and Wednesday’s calls it a new sale, both acquisition and retention reports become misleading.

Paddle uses delinquent churn for payment-related customer loss. For your own reporting, write down the exact point when an overdue account becomes a lost account: access ended, subscription cancelled, or another documented rule. Apply the same rule each month.

sections.title: A worked example: 20 overdue accounts, not 20 lost customers
sections.body:
Imagine 500 paying customers at the start of April. During April, 20 encounter overdue invoices. Twelve resolve the balance before your reporting cutoff. Eight meet your payment-related churn definition. The monthly delinquent customer churn rate is 8 ÷ 500 = 1.6%, not 20 ÷ 500 = 4%.

Those eight customers might represent very different subscription values. Report the recurring revenue they represent separately from the customer count. This example is illustrative; it is not a Rebound benchmark.

sections.title: Build a queue with an owner and an outcome
sections.body:
1. Identify the debt: use distinct subscription invoice IDs, not raw failure counts.
  2. Check today’s balance: remove paid or cancelled debt from the actionable queue.
  3. Choose a next step: eligible saved-card attempt, customer update, or manual review.
  4. Assign an owner: name the person responsible for unresolved cases.
  5. Close the loop: record payment, customer loss, or a reason collection stopped.

A week of failed attempts on one invoice should produce one accountable case, not a growing stack of unrelated alerts. Our reporting checklist shows how to reconcile the list.

sections.title: Track cohorts after the first decline
sections.body:
Group invoices by their first failure week, then revisit the same group after 7, 14, and 30 days. Record how much was collected and how much remains unresolved. Keeping the original group fixed makes it harder for newly failed invoices to hide improvements in older ones.

Separate recovery of old debt from continued subscription activity. An account can settle an old invoice and still cancel afterward. That payment belongs in your cash recovery result, but it does not automatically prove customer retention.

sections.title: Where Rebound fits
sections.body:
Rebound handles a specific action within that process: review date-filtered failed Stripe subscription payments, then deliberately start a run across eligible saved cards. It is not a cancellation survey, email sender, or guarantee that an overdue customer will stay.

Start with the involuntary churn guide for the broader problem, then use recovery metrics to measure the actual result.

title: How to reduce SaaS churn without mixing up the causes
description: A practical SaaS churn plan: separate cancellations from payment failures, prioritize the right accounts, and measure retention with consistent cohorts.
answer: Reduce SaaS churn by identifying why customers leave before choosing a fix. Product dissatisfaction, pricing friction, and failed subscription payments need different responses and separate outcome measures.

sections.title: Start with a cause, not a single churn percentage
sections.body:
A churn rate tells you how many relationships ended. It does not tell you whether to improve onboarding, change pricing, or repair billing. Start a weekly review with three buckets: intentional cancellation, payment-related loss, and unknown cause.

Use evidence rather than guessing. A cancellation survey, a support conversation, product activity, and an unpaid invoice can each add context. An inactive user who also has a declined card does not automatically belong in only one bucket. Keep an unknown category until someone investigates.

sections.title: Match each cause to a concrete action
sections.body:
• Customers never reach value: identify the first useful outcome and remove obstacles to it.
  • The plan no longer fits: explain available plan changes and clarify what customers lose or keep.
  • Support problems accumulate: review unresolved cases before asking customers to renew.
  • Payments fail: inspect unpaid invoices, available cards, and cases requiring customer action.

Do not send a product discount as the default answer to a billing problem. Someone who wants to stay but needs to update a card needs a clear payment path, not another sales pitch.

sections.title: Prioritize the next week of work
sections.body:
For each bucket, record affected customers, recurring revenue, a proposed action, and an owner. Choose one change you can evaluate against a fixed customer group. For example: give customers with unresolved billing issues a direct route to update payment details, then compare resolution with the prior process.

A small business can start with a spreadsheet. The important part is making each issue actionable and checking whether it was resolved. More dashboards do not compensate for cases nobody owns.

sections.title: Measure customer retention and money separately
sections.body:
Suppose ten customers cancel: nine pay $20 a month and one pays $2,000. A customer-count measure treats each equally; a revenue measure shows the concentration. Keep both. Also separate cash collected on overdue invoices from the recurring revenue of customers who remain active.

Gross and net revenue retention help distinguish losses from expansion. A business can have strong expansion and still lose customers it should have kept. Do not let upgrades erase the operational view of those losses.

sections.title: Build a payment-specific recovery lane
sections.body:
Payment-related cases deserve their own workflow because the customer may never have intended to cancel. Start with the original invoice, verify the remaining balance, and choose between a controlled saved-card attempt and customer follow-up. Keep communication and collection coordinated.

Rebound supports that saved-card lane for Stripe subscription invoices. It does not replace product retention work or guarantee an improvement in total churn. Read how to measure delinquent churn before claiming that recovered cash equals saved customers.

sources: Stripe: net and gross revenue retention

title: Gross vs. net revenue retention: formulas and a worked example
description: Calculate GRR and NRR with a simple SaaS cohort example. Learn where payment recovery belongs and why collected overdue cash is not automatically new MRR.
answer: Gross revenue retention measures how much starting recurring revenue remains after churn and downgrades. Net revenue retention also includes expansion from that same starting customer cohort. Neither is simply the cash you collected this month.

sections.title: Use the same starting customer cohort
sections.body:
Choose a period and list the customers paying at its beginning. Measure the recurring revenue from those customers at the end. Keep customers acquired during the period out of this calculation: acquisition is important, but it answers a different question.

Use consistent treatment for currency, discounts, usage-based charges, and overdue accounts. Your billing system’s MRR definition may differ from cash receipts. Write the rule down before comparing months or comparing your number with someone else’s.

sections.title: The formulas
sections.body:
GRR

(Starting MRR − churned MRR − contraction MRR) ÷ starting MRR × 100

NRR

(Starting MRR − churned MRR − contraction MRR + expansion MRR) ÷ starting MRR × 100

Contraction means recurring revenue lost through downgrades or similar reductions. Expansion means additional recurring revenue from existing customers. With these definitions, GRR cannot exceed 100%; NRR can. If starting MRR is zero, the ratio is undefined, not zero.

sections.title: A $50,000 cohort example
sections.body:
A SaaS business starts with $50,000 in MRR from its existing customers. It loses $2,000 to cancellations and $1,000 to downgrades, while existing customers add $4,000 in expansion. GRR is $47,000 ÷ $50,000 = 94%. NRR is $51,000 ÷ $50,000 = 102%.

The business grew within that cohort overall, but still lost $3,000 of recurring revenue before expansion. That loss remains worth investigating. These are made-up numbers for explaining the calculation, not performance claims.

sections.title: Where recovered payments fit
sections.body:
Suppose an old $500 invoice is paid today. That is $500 of collected cash. It does not necessarily add $500 to MRR: the invoice might cover an earlier service period, include tax, or belong to a customer whose subscription has ended.

If resolving a failure prevents customer loss under your reporting rules, the recurring subscription value may remain in the retained cohort. Record that outcome separately from the invoice payment. Do not add the recovered invoice total directly to NRR’s expansion term.

sections.title: Create a monthly reconciliation
sections.body:
1. Freeze the starting cohort and starting MRR.
  2. Record cancellations, contractions, and expansions for that cohort.
  3. Apply the same overdue-account policy to every period.
  4. Keep a separate ledger of recovered invoices and collection dates.
  5. Explain adjustments rather than silently rewriting earlier results.

Use payment recovery metrics for collection operations and the recovery opportunity calculator for scenarios. Neither replaces a full revenue-retention report.

title: Payment recovery metrics: measure money, invoices, and customers
description: Define invoice and amount recovery rates, fixed cohorts, attribution, and time to recovery. Includes an example that avoids counting repeated declines as lost revenue.
answer: Measure payment recovery using a fixed set of failed invoices and confirmed outcomes. Report recovered money, paid invoices, and retained customers separately; repeated attempts are not additional debt.

sections.title: Start with a fixed population
sections.body:
A recovery rate needs a denominator you can explain. Choose a group of distinct invoices, such as subscription invoices with a first failure in October, and freeze their balances at the chosen starting point. Decide whether the report covers every failed invoice or only the invoices eligible for a particular tool.

Those are different rates. If 100 invoices failed but only 40 had eligible cards, success on 20 is 20% of all failed invoices and 50% of the eligible group. Neither number is wrong if the label is clear. Leaving out the denominator makes both easy to misuse.

sections.title: Keep an amount rate and an invoice rate
sections.body:
Invoice recovery rate

Distinct invoices paid from the starting group ÷ invoices in that group × 100

Amount recovery rate

Confirmed amount collected toward that group’s starting balances ÷ those starting balances × 100

Count each invoice once in the invoice rate. Handle partial payments explicitly in the amount rate. Separate currencies rather than adding unlike units, and state whether taxes and credits are included.

sections.title: A small example that exposes misleading totals
sections.body:
Ten invoices have a combined unpaid balance of $1,000. Four invoices worth $600 get paid. The invoice recovery rate is 40%; the amount recovery rate is 60%. The same result supports both numbers because larger invoices recovered more often.

If those ten invoices produced 35 failed card attempts, the starting debt is still $1,000. A report that sums the amount of every failure would inflate the opportunity. These figures illustrate reporting mechanics, not expected recovery.

sections.title: Track time and attribution
sections.body:
Measure elapsed time from the first failure to confirmed payment, then compare like-for-like cohorts. A newly failed invoice and an invoice overdue for six months should not be treated as equally mature recovery opportunities.

Separate payments linked to your tool’s attempts from payments that happened through another route, such as a customer paying directly. A payment occurring after a run is not enough to prove that the run caused it. Use the Stripe attribution checklist to establish a stronger trail.

sections.title: Use cash and retention reports together
sections.body:
Collected cash answers whether an invoice was settled. Customer retention answers whether the relationship continued under a documented definition. Review active subscription status and later billing periods before presenting a collection as a saved customer.

Rebound’s Insights view shows recorded recoveries and monthly detail. Use it alongside the original Stripe invoice and your own retention reporting. For planning rather than measurement, use the scenario calculator; its assumptions are not observed performance.

title: Stripe Smart Retries vs. saved-card fallback
description: Understand retry timing, payment-method priority, and saved-card fallback. Use a decision checklist to coordinate Stripe recovery with an additional collection tool.
answer: Stripe Smart Retries chooses when to retry eligible failed payments. Saved-card fallback chooses another eligible stored card to try. Compare timing, card selection, and reporting separately rather than assuming they are the same feature.

sections.title: Timing and card selection answer different questions
sections.body:
A payment that failed this morning might succeed later. A different saved card might also work. These are separate hypotheses: wait for a better moment, or choose another eligible method. Your billing process needs to be clear about which action it is taking.

Stripe documents an ordered set of subscription and customer defaults for retries. Smart Retries optimizes timing; the presence of several cards on a customer does not by itself mean a round-robin attempt across every stored card.

sections.title: An illustrative three-card invoice
sections.body:
A customer owes $96 and has cards A, B, and C. Card A fails. A timed retry strategy may attempt collection later using the applicable configured method. A saved-card fallback strategy may try eligible card B and, if necessary, eligible card C.

If card B pays the invoice, the process should stop. The goal is to settle the $96 debt once, not to test every card. If a result is still processing or uncertain, pause the invoice for verification rather than treating uncertainty as a decline.

sections.title: What to check before combining tools
sections.body:
• Ownership: which system can start a charge, and when?
  • Scope: which original invoices are eligible?
  • Current state: does the tool recheck payment before its next attempt?
  • Card eligibility: what happens with duplicates, expired cards, or methods requiring customer action?
  • Evidence: can you connect a successful outcome to the payment request?

A second recovery tool should not be a second uncoordinated collection process. Test in a non-live environment and review your retry settings before using both.

sections.title: Where Rebound differs
sections.body:
Rebound is an operator-started recovery workspace. Review failed subscription payments for a date range and click Start recovery for the eligible invoices. It works through eligible distinct saved cards once per invoice in that run and stops on payment or when the run cannot continue safely.

It does not provide Smart Retries’ timing model, dunning email campaigns, or guaranteed recovery. Opening the list does not charge customers. Starting a later run is a separate collection decision, so do not interpret the per-run limit as a lifetime limit.

sections.title: Choose based on the unresolved problem
sections.body:
If nobody has reviewed your current retry and email settings, start there. If the recurring problem is unpaid invoices where customers already have other eligible saved cards, inspect the different-card workflow. If authentication is required, use a customer-facing resolution path.

Evaluate tools with a fixed invoice cohort. Compare actual confirmed collections, not a headline recovery percentage from a different business.

sections.title: When the same card keeps returning
sections.body:
If a replacement exists but retries still target the old card, inspect the effective defaults before changing timing. The same-card diagnostic walks through that mismatch. For messaging and unresolved accounts, use the dunning checklist.

Saved-card fallback is also advertised by other recovery vendors. Read the public-documentation comparisons with FlyCode and Stunning when evaluating scope; this feature alone is not exclusive to Rebound.

title: How to retry a failed Stripe invoice with a different saved card
description: A step-by-step workflow for an unpaid subscription invoice with multiple saved cards. Check eligibility, stop on payment, and keep the original invoice reference.
answer: To retry with another saved card, work from the existing unpaid invoice, check that the customer’s alternative card is eligible, attempt that invoice, and verify the result before considering another card.

sections.title: Find the debt before choosing the card
sections.body:
Open the original subscription invoice and confirm its customer, currency, remaining amount, and current payment state. A historical decline can remain visible after the balance has been paid. Do not create a new standalone charge just because a failure list still contains the old attempt.

Stripe’s invoice payment API supports attempting payment on an existing invoice with a specified payment method. That establishes the technical path; it does not mean every saved card is eligible for every payment or that you should retry without reviewing the account.

sections.title: Separate saved from eligible
sections.body:
Three saved payment-method records do not necessarily mean three useful attempts. You might find expired cards, duplicate records for the same physical card, or a method that cannot be used for this collection. An authentication requirement can also mean the customer must return.

Keep the total saved-card count and the eligible retry count separate. That distinction helps an operator understand why an account with several cards may still need follow-up. Avoid asking customers to send full card details to support; use a hosted update path instead.

sections.title: Use a stop-on-payment sequence
sections.body:
1. Verify that the original invoice still has an intended unpaid balance.
  2. Select the next eligible distinct saved card under your collection policy.
  3. Attempt payment of that invoice.
  4. Confirm the outcome against the invoice and payment record.
  5. Stop if paid; pause if processing or uncertain; continue only when a confirmed failure and policy permit it.

If cards A and B fail and card C succeeds, the outcome is one paid invoice with three attempts. If A succeeds, B and C should not be charged for that invoice.

sections.title: How Rebound handles the repeated work
sections.body:
Collections loads the last 15 days of failed subscription payments by default. Change the date range if needed, review unpaid invoices and saved-card counts, then start the filtered recovery run. Rebound works invoice by invoice instead of requiring a click for each customer and card.

Each eligible physical card is tried once per invoice in that run. Successful rows turn green. Card-attempt history and invoice references let you inspect what happened. Rebound holds uncertain results for review rather than blindly moving to another charge.

sections.title: Do not confuse this payment with future renewals
sections.body:
Paying an existing invoice and choosing the default for future renewals are separate tasks. After resolving the current debt, review where the subscription’s intended payment method is configured. A customer who updates billing details should know whether that change affects the current invoice, later invoices, or both.

For that distinction, read retry timing versus fallback. For a result that needs customer verification, use the authentication guide.

sections.title: A worked invoice walkthrough
sections.body:
Illustrative walkthrough—not live account evidence. Invoice INV-1041 has $96 outstanding. Card A fails. Card B pays the original invoice. Card C is not attempted. There is one $96 collection, not three debts.
  1. Open the original invoice and confirm $96 remains due.
  2. Review the customer’s distinct eligible cards and the latest decline advice.
  3. Coordinate existing retries before starting collection.
  4. Attempt the existing invoice using the chosen eligible method; inspect the returned outcome.
  5. Stop once paid. If the outcome is uncertain, reconcile it before another card.
  6. Record the invoice, request reference, paid amount, and next subscription action.

A technical team can use Stripe’s invoice pay endpoint with a customer-owned payment method; this is an actual charging action. In Rebound, review the list and deliberately start the run instead of performing this sequence invoice by invoice.

A new customer default might not replace a subscription-level default. Use the same-card diagnostic if the old card keeps returning. Changing future billing preferences is separate from collecting this invoice.
