title: Stripe past_due vs. unpaid: what each subscription status means
description: Understand Stripe subscription status versus invoice status. Review overdue accounts without confusing a failed charge, unpaid debt, and a cancelled subscription.
answer: past_due and unpaid describe subscription states, while open, paid, uncollectible, and void describe invoices. Read the subscription, the relevant invoices, and your billing settings together before deciding what remains collectible.

sections.title: Three records, three questions
sections.body:
The subscription describes the ongoing billing relationship. The invoice records an amount billed. A payment attempt records an effort to collect it. One subscription can have several invoices, and one invoice can have several attempts.

This matters when support asks, “Why is the customer still unpaid?” A successful payment on one old invoice may not settle every outstanding obligation. Conversely, a historical failed attempt is not evidence that money remains due today.

sections.title: What the subscription labels tell you
sections.body:
Stripe uses past_due when relevant invoice payment has not been settled under the account’s configuration. unpaid can be the configured outcome after unsuccessful recovery. Retry behavior and the invoices governing subscription status depend on billing settings.

Do not assume that paying any single invoice automatically restores a subscription. Check the status-resolution policy and the remaining applicable invoices. The current Stripe documentation describes these settings; your own configuration is the source of truth for the account.

sections.title: Review an account in a useful order
sections.body:
1. Confirm you are looking at the correct customer and subscription.
  2. List the invoices still carrying a balance.
  3. Separate old failures from currently payable debt.
  4. Check whether a payment is in progress or needs customer action.
  5. Resolve the intended debt and then verify subscription status.

Keep a short note when the outcome differs from what support expected. That note can explain whether an old invoice remains, an invoice was cancelled, or the account needs another action.

sections.title: An example with more than one invoice
sections.body:
A customer has an unpaid September invoice and an unpaid October invoice. The October payment is collected today. Support should verify the September balance and the configured subscription status rule rather than declaring the entire account fixed solely from October’s receipt.

The collection report should record the October payment once. Whether the customer is retained or access is restored is a separate question. This distinction prevents your recovery total from quietly becoming an inaccurate customer-retention total.

sections.title: Where Rebound helps
sections.body:
Rebound shows failed subscription payments grouped around their invoices and checks current eligibility before collection. It does not make every visible historical failure actionable. Read the invoice-state guide for written-off and cancelled debt.

After a run, inspect the original invoice in Stripe as well as the app result. For reporting, use a defined date range and matching population rather than comparing unrelated screen totals.

seoTitle: Stripe past_due vs. unpaid: subscription statuses

title: Stripe decline codes: choose the next action after a failed payment
description: Turn common subscription decline codes into a practical triage workflow. Separate customer action, card replacement, and outcomes that need verification.
answer: A decline code helps explain a failed card attempt; it is not a universal instruction to retry. Read the code and payment state, then choose between customer action, an eligible alternative method, or review.

sections.title: Triage the outcome before the wording
sections.body:
Start by confirming whether the attempt is actually a failure. A timeout in your app is not the same as an issuer declining the card. If the payment is processing or its result is unclear, verify it before another collection attempt.

Then record the original invoice, the method used, the decline information, and the time. The code explains that attempt. The invoice balance tells you whether there is still a debt to resolve.

sections.title: Common codes and practical next steps
sections.body:
insufficient_funds
Available funds were insufficient. Give the customer a clear route to another suitable method; do not assume immediate repetition will fix it.
expired_card
Use a replacement or another eligible card rather than repeatedly presenting the expired one.
authentication_required
Route the customer to complete the required verification. A background retry cannot perform the customer’s challenge.
do_not_honor or generic_decline
The message does not provide a dependable detailed explanation. Avoid inventing one; use an appropriate customer or issuer follow-up.
duplicate_transaction
Check for a recent existing payment before trying again.

These summaries cover selected codes, not the full decline catalog. Stripe’s reference below provides the exact current meanings and advice.

sections.title: What to tell the customer
sections.body:
Use simple language: which subscription invoice needs attention, the remaining amount, and one secure way to resolve it. Do not turn internal risk signals into accusations. A customer-facing message should help someone pay, not reveal sensitive screening details or imply misconduct.

Keep the message synchronized with the balance. An email asking for payment after the invoice has already been paid is a fast way to lose trust. Our email templates include placeholders for the amount, invoice, and resolution link.

sections.title: When another saved card belongs in the workflow
sections.body:
An eligible alternative saved card can be useful when the intended debt is still outstanding and your collection policy permits using it. Saved-card recovery is not a way to bypass authentication requirements or ignore restrictions.

In Rebound, review the eligible invoices and start a controlled run. Each eligible distinct card is tried once per invoice in that run. Paid invoices stop; cases with uncertain outcomes need review. See the different-card guide for the sequence.

sections.title: Review patterns without losing invoice detail
sections.body:
Each week, group unresolved invoices by next action: replacement needed, customer authentication, confirmed decline, no eligible saved method, and uncertain result. Assign an owner to each group. Keep invoice-level references so support can investigate an individual case.

Report distinct invoices and amounts, not just the number of decline events. A rising event count might mean the same debt was attempted more often rather than more customers becoming overdue.

sections.title: Go deeper on two common troubleshooting paths
sections.body: For low-funds failures, use the decline code 51 checklist. For a non-specific issuer refusal, use the do_not_honor diagnostic. The two are not the same diagnosis. Verify the actual code, network, and advice before choosing the next action.

sources: Stripe: decline codes and next actions
seoTitle: Stripe decline codes: practical next actions

title: Stripe authentication_required: why another background retry may not help
description: Understand subscription payments that require customer authentication. Learn the difference between a declined card, an unfinished challenge, and a confirmed payment.
answer: authentication_required means the payment needs customer verification. Direct the customer to an appropriate payment or authentication flow and verify completion; repeatedly retrying in the background does not complete that step for them.

sections.title: The customer may still want to pay
sections.body:
A renewal can fail even when a customer has a usable card and wants to keep the product. The customer is absent during the background payment, but the bank may require an action they must complete. Treat the case as an unfinished payment journey, not an immediate cancellation.

Stripe’s subscription documentation distinguishes a payment needing action from a completed payment. The practical question is whether the customer has a secure, working way to finish that action.

sections.title: Give support a short resolution checklist
sections.body:
1. Find the original invoice and confirm it remains unpaid.
  2. Check the current payment state rather than relying only on an older error message.
  3. Provide the appropriate hosted payment or verification route.
  4. Explain the amount and subscription the action relates to.
  5. Confirm payment before closing the case or changing access.

A screenshot saying the customer opened a link is not payment confirmation. Keep the invoice reference and check the final result.

sections.title: Use a customer message with one action
sections.body:
Your payment for [subscription] needs one more step. Please use [secure payment link] to confirm payment of [amount] for invoice [number]. If you already completed it, contact [support] and we’ll check the result.

Replace every placeholder, verify the destination, and send it through your approved customer communication process. Do not request full card details or verification codes in a support message. The template is wording to adapt, not an email sent by Rebound.

sections.title: Keep recovery tools coordinated
sections.body:
Before another operator or system attempts the same invoice, make sure it can see whether the existing payment is complete, still processing, or awaiting customer action. An unclear result belongs in review. Otherwise two teams can act on different snapshots of the same debt.

Rebound focuses on eligible saved-card recovery and records run outcomes. It does not perform a customer’s verification challenge. A row that needs review is a useful signal to investigate, not a reason to assume the tool should keep charging.

sections.title: Confirm the full account outcome
sections.body:
After the intended invoice is paid, check whether other balances or subscription conditions remain. Separately confirm any product-access change your business requires. A paid invoice and an active ongoing subscription answer different questions.

Use the subscription status guide for that distinction, and the decline guide when the problem is a different type of failure.

sources: Stripe: decline codes and next actions
seoTitle: Stripe authentication_required: what to do next

title: Failed payment email templates for SaaS subscriptions
description: Copy and adapt three clear payment-failure emails: first notice, card update, and follow-up. Includes a checklist to stop reminders after payment.
answer: A useful failed-payment email states what remains due, identifies the subscription, and gives the customer one secure action. Check the invoice before sending and stop reminders when the balance is resolved.

sections.title: First notice: explain the problem without blaming the customer
sections.body:
Subject: A payment needs attention for [product]

Hi [name],

We couldn’t complete the [amount] payment for [subscription], invoice [number]. Your subscription payment needs attention.

Please review it here: [secure invoice or billing link].

If you need help, reply to [support address]. We’ll help you check what happened.

[Team name]

This is a template, not an actual notice. Replace the fields and verify the unpaid balance before use. Do not claim that access has ended unless that is true under your policy.

sections.title: Card update: ask for a specific fix
sections.body:
Subject: Please update your payment method for [product]

Hi [name],

Invoice [number] for [amount] is still unpaid. Please update your payment method through [secure billing link] so we can resolve it.

If you already updated your card, let us know at [support address] and we’ll check the invoice before taking further action.

[Team name]

Use this when a method update is an appropriate next step. Stripe’s customer portal can provide payment-detail management. Confirm how your integration applies an update to the current invoice and future renewals.

sections.title: Follow-up: give a real deadline, not invented urgency
sections.body:
Subject: Follow-up on your unpaid [product] invoice

Hi [name],

We’re following up on invoice [number], with [amount] still due. You can review and resolve it at [secure billing link].

[If applicable: Under our billing policy, access changes on [actual date].]

If something looks wrong, contact [support address] before that date so we can help.

[Team name]

Remove the bracketed access sentence if no verified deadline applies. A fake countdown may create pressure, but it also creates confusion and support problems.

sections.title: Before sending any of these emails
sections.body:
• Check current invoice status and balance, not only the original failure.
  • Use a recognizable sender and the correct customer contact.
  • Verify that the secure link resolves to the intended billing workflow.
  • Avoid full card numbers, bank details, and internal risk explanations.
  • Do not send a second email sequence if another tool already owns follow-up.
  • Stop or adjust the sequence after payment, cancellation, or another final resolution.

Stripe provides configurable recovery emails. Review what is already enabled before adding manual reminders or another platform. The right cadence depends on your billing policy and account context; these templates do not prescribe a universal schedule.

sections.title: Use saved-card recovery and email for different jobs
sections.body:
Some invoices can be resolved through an eligible saved-card attempt. Others need a new method, authentication, or a customer conversation. Match the next action to the case instead of sending the same message for every decline.

Rebound does not send these email campaigns. It handles operator-started saved-card collection and traceability. Read dunning versus card fallback to plan how the two workflows should cooperate.

sections.title: Suppress messages against the current invoice state
sections.body:
Before each send, check whether the invoice remains outstanding and whether another customer action is already in progress. Stop unpaid reminders after confirmed resolution; route unknown outcomes for review. A historical failure event alone is not enough to justify another email.

Assign one system to own each message type. If Stripe, your app, and a recovery vendor all react to the same failure, the customer can receive duplicate or conflicting instructions. Test suppression with an invoice that becomes paid between scheduling and sending.

Rebound does not send these messages. Use the templates in your existing communication system or Stripe’s supported settings, and coordinate those settings with the complete dunning workflow.

seoTitle: Failed payment email templates for SaaS

title: How to build a failed-payment report that matches Stripe
description: Reconcile Stripe failure counts with unpaid invoices. Check dates, timezone, pagination, duplicates, current balances, and recovered payments before comparing totals.
answer: To reconcile a failed-payment report with Stripe, use the same account, mode, dates, timezone, and record type. Then group attempts by invoice and check current balances. A failure-event count and an unpaid-invoice count will often differ.

sections.title: Agree on the question before comparing numbers
sections.body:
“What failed this month?” and “What is unpaid today?” are different questions. A payment may fail twice during the month and later succeed. That creates failure history but no remaining balance on that invoice.

Start the report with a plain-English definition: subscription payment failures during a date window, grouped by original invoice, with the current remaining balance. If you want raw attempts instead, label them as attempts. A dashboard showing 33 attempts and a report showing 25 invoices are not necessarily missing eight invoices.

sections.title: Check six common causes of a mismatch
sections.body:
1. Account and mode: compare the same Stripe account and live or test environment.
  2. Time boundaries: use the same timezone and inclusive calendar-date rules.
  3. Record type: distinguish events, payments, invoices, and subscriptions.
  4. Pagination: finish the scan; an initial page is not the entire result.
  5. Grouping: consolidate attempts belonging to one invoice.
  6. Current state: label paid, voided, written-off, and unresolved invoices separately.

Reconcile these differences explicitly before concluding a tool has lost records. If there is still a gap, compare invoice IDs directly.

sections.title: Use a minimal reconciliation worksheet
sections.body:
For each invoice, keep the customer reference, invoice ID, currency, remaining amount, first and last failure in range, number of matched attempts, current state, and next action. Keep a separate list of raw attempts if you need to audit how the invoice group was produced.

For example, three declines against a $40 invoice represent three failures but only $40 of outstanding debt. Once paid, that invoice still belongs in the period’s failure history while its current amount due becomes zero. Preserve both facts.

sections.title: Distinguish finding records from starting collection
sections.body:
A completed report is not itself permission to charge every row. Some invoices cannot or should not be retried. Review the intended debt, current payment state, saved methods, and collection policy before acting.

Rebound separates the unpaid invoice view from full failure history. It automatically loads the last 15 days and lets you change dates. Collection starts only through the deliberate run action; it is not triggered by reading the report.

sections.title: Close the reconciliation after recovery
sections.body:
Keep the original selection so the before-and-after comparison uses the same invoices. Record confirmed payment separately from failed or uncertain attempts. Do not silently remove paid rows from historical reporting and then lose the explanation for the balance change.

Use fixed-cohort metrics for results and request-level evidence when identifying what your recovery tool collected.

sections.title: Reconcile a small example before the whole month
sections.body:
Suppose your failure export contains 33 records. In an illustrative reconciliation, those records refer to 25 distinct subscription invoices. Three have since been paid, one was voided, and two have no usable saved method. You would report 33 historical failure records, 25 distinct invoices with failures, 21 currently unpaid non-void invoices, and at most 19 candidates before other eligibility checks. These are different questions, not interchangeable counts.

This example is not your account’s data. Keep void and paid records in history rather than deleting them to force totals to match.

  1. Use the same account, live/test mode, time zone, and failure-event interval on both sides.
  2. Export all pages of matching records; record the extraction time.
  3. Group by the original invoice ID, preserving the number of failures.
  4. Read today’s invoice state separately from the historical event window.
  5. Record every inclusion or exclusion reason.

Use a start-inclusive, end-exclusive timestamp interval when joining event exports, and convert a calendar end date to the next day in the chosen time zone. Do not assume every day is exactly 24 hours across daylight-saving changes.

sections.title: Download the reconciliation worksheet
sections.body:
Download reconciliation CSV →

The empty worksheet contains invoice and subscription references, failure timestamps, the report time zone, failure count, current balance, saved-card counts, eligibility reason, and reconciliation notes. Fill it with your own exports in a private workspace. It does not fetch Stripe data or initiate charges.

Keep separate currencies separate. Record the historical failure population first, then derive today’s recovery candidates. Use the attribution guide when an invoice subsequently becomes paid.

seoTitle: How to reconcile a Stripe failed-payment report

title: How to verify a recovered payment in Stripe
description: Trace recovery from a tool’s run to the original Stripe invoice and API request. Avoid claiming every payment after a run was recovered by that tool.
answer: Verify a recovery by matching the original invoice and confirmed payment with the collection tool’s attempt record. Stripe request logs can provide stronger evidence of origin than an invoice-paid event or a matching timestamp alone.

sections.title: A paid event does not name the whole cause
sections.body:
An invoice can become paid through several routes: a background billing process, an operator, the customer, or another collection tool. The fact that it was paid after your run started does not establish that your tool caused the payment.

Start with the tool’s run ID, invoice ID, attempt time, recorded outcome, and Stripe references available for the attempt. Then confirm the invoice’s actual payment. If the evidence cannot be connected, label the origin unconfirmed rather than forcing it into an attributed total.

sections.title: Inspect the original invoice and related request
sections.body:
1. Open the invoice linked from the recovery result.
  2. Verify the customer, currency, amount, and final payment state.
  3. Locate the related payment and available request log in Stripe Workbench.
  4. Compare the request endpoint, time, and request identifier with the tool’s evidence.
  5. Retain the references so someone else can reproduce the check.

Stripe associates API requests with request identifiers. The event object can also carry request-related information. What appears depends on how the action originated and what records are available; do not assume every event has a usable origin label.

sections.title: What an invoice-pay request proves—and what it does not
sections.body:
A request to pay the intended invoice, linked to a successful payment and the tool’s attempt, is useful attribution evidence. An HTTP success code alone is not the full reconciliation: verify what the returned invoice and related payment actually show.

An idempotency key can help correlate an operation, but a memorable prefix is not a universal product badge. Do not assume Stripe will display “Recovered by Rebound” unless a specific verified integration field says so. API key identity and timestamps support an investigation; neither alone settles every case.

sections.title: Keep a clean recovery ledger
sections.body:
Store the invoice, currency, confirmed collected amount, collection date, run reference, and relevant payment/request references. Separate confirmed tool-attributed collections from customer-paid or otherwise unattributed outcomes. Keep refunds and later adjustments distinguishable from the original collection.

For a monthly finance review, someone should be able to select a reported recovery and follow it back to the original debt and collection evidence. This is more useful than a large headline total with no drill-down.

sections.title: How to use Rebound’s views
sections.body:
Review card-by-card run outcomes in Collections and the recorded monthly payments in Insights. Follow the invoice reference to Stripe for verification. These views support traceability; they do not mean every payment in the connected Stripe account is attributable to Rebound.

Read the metrics guide before reporting a percentage. The Porter Metrics customer example clearly separates a customer-reported result from a public transaction audit.

sections.title: An evidence trail you can reproduce
sections.body:
1. Select one collected invoice in the run results.
  2. Open that original invoice in the correct Stripe account and mode.
  3. Find its relevant payment and request log around the run’s attempt time.
  4. Compare the request ID, endpoint, invoice, method, and result with your tool’s record.
  5. Verify the paid amount and any later refunds or disputes separately.

A matching POST /v1/invoices/{invoice}/pay request is useful evidence of an invoice payment attempt. A shared API key or a nearby timestamp alone cannot identify the caller. A paid_out_of_band operation is not proof of a Stripe card charge. Check the full context.

In the event, request references may help connect the change to its API request. Some events are not caused by a direct API call. Do not assume an event label automatically names Rebound.

Illustrative chain: run-example → in_example → req_example → confirmed invoice payment. These are placeholders, not redacted transaction records. Public customer-level proof should only be added after the actual records are reconciled and approved for disclosure.

sections.title: Download an attribution ledger
sections.body:
Download attribution CSV →

For each invoice, record the run, attempt time, Stripe request reference, confirmed collection, currency, attribution decision, reviewer, and later adjustments. Use “unknown” when evidence is incomplete rather than forcing every paid invoice into the recovered total.

Distinguish tool-attributed collection from incremental recovery: even a well-matched request does not prove the customer or another retry would never have paid. An incremental claim needs a comparison design, not just an API log.

seoTitle: Verify payment recovery in Stripe: an audit checklist

title: Why Stripe keeps retrying the same card after a payment fails
description: A new card on the customer does not always change the subscription default. Diagnose repeated Stripe retries and choose the right invoice recovery action.
answer: Stripe can keep retrying a subscription’s default card even after another card is saved on the customer. Check which default controls the retry before changing the schedule or assuming the new card will be selected.

sections.title: Start with one unpaid invoice, not the customer’s card count
sections.body:
Open the original invoice and confirm its current balance and latest payment outcome. Then inspect its subscription and customer. A count of three saved cards answers how many methods exist; it does not tell you which one a scheduled retry selects.

Write down four things: invoice reference, last attempted card, subscription default, and customer billing default. If those references differ, investigate the mismatch before attempting collection.

sections.title: The subscription default can take priority
sections.body:
Stripe documents a retry order: subscription default payment method, subscription default source, customer billing default payment method, then the legacy customer default source. Updating only a lower-priority default can leave the subscription retrying the previous method. See Stripe’s payment method ordering.

Illustrative example. A subscription defaults to card A. The customer adds card B and makes it their customer-level default. The subscription still points to A. A saved replacement and the effective subscription default are different facts.

sections.title: Separate three decisions: card, timing, and customer action
sections.body:
1. Card: verify which eligible method should pay this invoice.
  2. Timing: review the existing retry policy and other active recovery tools.
  3. Customer action: identify cases needing authentication, corrected details, or issuer contact.

Do not solve an authentication problem by simply increasing attempts. Our authentication guide explains that branch. For the broader timing-versus-method distinction, read Smart Retries vs. saved-card fallback.

sections.title: Recover this invoice without confusing future renewals
sections.body:
A one-off attempt on the existing invoice and a change to the subscription’s future default are separate actions. Stripe’s invoice-payment API supports specifying a method belonging to that invoice’s customer. Verify the result against the original invoice rather than creating a second debt.

Use the different-card walkthrough for the operational sequence. Record any intended renewal-default change separately so a one-time recovery does not silently become a permanent billing preference.

sections.title: Where Rebound fits
sections.body:
Rebound lets an operator review failed subscription payments, then deliberately start a run across eligible saved cards. Each eligible distinct card is tried once per invoice in that run, stopping on payment. Opening the list does not charge customers.

This is a collection workflow, not a promise that every stored card is usable. Rebound does not replace Stripe’s authentication requirements or supply an email campaign. Review connection and collection controls before connecting.

title: Stripe dunning: configure retries, emails, and the next action
description: Set up Stripe dunning around retries, failed-payment emails, customer updates, and unresolved invoices. See where saved-card recovery fits.
answer: Stripe dunning is the process of following up on overdue subscription payments using retries, customer messages, and a defined outcome when collection fails. Configure the native tools first, then identify the work your team still needs to handle.

sections.title: Give each part of the workflow an owner
sections.body:
Start with a simple operating rule: every unpaid subscription invoice needs a next action and an owner. That action might be a scheduled retry, a customer update, a deliberate saved-card run, or review. An invoice waiting for authentication should not disappear into the same bucket as one with a usable alternative card.

Dunning and saved-card fallback solve overlapping but different jobs. The objective is one coherent process, not several tools independently contacting or charging the same account.

sections.title: Check the native retry settings
sections.body:
In Stripe, open Billing → Revenue recovery → Retries. Review your actual retry count, window, and final subscription outcome. Smart Retries chooses timing within the configured policy; do not assume another account’s settings apply to yours.

Document who can change this policy and which other systems can attempt collection. Use the same-card diagnostic when the problem is method selection rather than timing.

sections.title: Configure a way for the customer to resolve the failure
sections.body:
Stripe provides failed-payment emails and payment-confirmation messages with hosted recovery options. Check the relevant email settings, branding, destination, and recipient details. Recurring invoice reminders for manually sent invoices are a separate setting from failed automatic-card notifications.

For your own messages, use the failed-payment templates. Send customers to a secure billing page; do not ask them to email card details. Test the path from notification to invoice resolution.

sections.title: A practical review checklist
sections.body:
• Before the next attempt: check the current invoice balance and latest outcome.
  • If a method needs attention: assign the card update or authentication request to an owner.
  • If another eligible card exists: choose a coordinated collection workflow.
  • After payment: remove the invoice from unpaid follow-up and verify future subscription status separately.
  • If unresolved: follow the access and cancellation policy you actually communicated.

Never treat a generic decline as proof the customer intended to cancel.

sections.title: What Rebound adds—and what it does not
sections.body:
Rebound focuses on deliberate, invoice-level collection across eligible saved cards, with card-attempt and invoice results. It does not send dunning emails or operate an automatic background recovery schedule. Keep your customer communication and other retry policies coordinated with any run.

For a more complete communication suite, evaluate that requirement explicitly. The Stunning comparison explains a different product scope; the FlyCode comparison covers a broader recovery platform.

sections.title: Measure the process without inflating recovery
sections.body:
Fix a cohort of distinct original invoices. Track their opening balances, collection outcomes, and who caused each payment. Failed attempts, paid invoices, collected cash, and retained customers are separate measures.

Use the recovery metrics guide and the attribution worksheet before presenting a recovery percentage. A paid invoice does not by itself prove incremental recovery over Stripe.

title: Decline code 51: an insufficient-funds checklist for subscriptions
description: Handle card decline code 51 in a subscription business: verify the network response, inspect the invoice, and choose a customer update or eligible alternative card.
answer: For Visa card payments, network decline code 51 means insufficient funds. In Stripe, also inspect the normalized decline code and any retry advice. A low-funds failure is a payment problem to resolve, not automatic evidence of customer churn.

sections.title: Confirm what the code refers to
sections.body:
A network response code and a Stripe decline code are different fields. Stripe’s network reference maps Visa 51 to insufficient funds; the card network matters when reading raw codes. Check the actual payment record instead of translating a screenshot label in isolation.

This guide is for subscription operators. If your own card was declined, contact the merchant or card issuer; Rebound cannot view or fix your personal bank balance.

sections.title: Use an invoice-first checklist
sections.body:
1. Find the subscription’s original invoice and current unpaid balance.
  2. Check whether another process or the customer has already paid it.
  3. Read the latest failure and available advice rather than relying on an older event.
  4. Review other saved methods for eligibility and authorization.
  5. Choose the next action and document the outcome.

Keep the amount and currency intact. Repeated failures on the same invoice do not create additional revenue exposure.

sections.title: Choose an action that could change the result
sections.body:
Stripe’s guidance for insufficient_funds points to an alternative payment method. An eligible different saved card may provide a collection path; its existence does not guarantee success. If the customer needs to update billing or resolve a restriction, use a secure customer-facing path.

Review advice and existing retry activity before making another attempt. Avoid a rapid loop against the same unchanged method. If a payment outcome is uncertain, reconcile it before trying another card.

sections.title: Illustrative case: one debt, two cards
sections.body:
Example, not a customer result. A $96 subscription invoice fails on card A with insufficient funds. Card B is saved and eligible. The operator verifies that $96 remains due, starts the selected recovery workflow, and B pays the original invoice. The invoice is now paid; further cards are unnecessary.

If B fails too, the debt remains the same $96. Record the attempts and the unresolved next action, rather than counting $192 in failed revenue.

sections.title: Move from troubleshooting to a repeatable process
sections.body:
Rebound handles the repeated card-by-card work after an operator starts a run. It stops for an invoice when paid or when its eligible cards are exhausted; unknown outcomes need review. It is not a way to override an issuer restriction.

Continue with the different-card workflow or a customer follow-up template. Reconcile the result before calling the customer retained.

sources: Stripe: card declines and retry advice

title: Stripe do_not_honor: what subscription operators should do next
description: Diagnose a Stripe do_not_honor decline without guessing the bank’s reason. Check the original invoice, retry advice, and customer-action path.
answer: Stripe’s do_not_honor decline means the issuer declined the payment without providing a specific reason. It does not identify a single cause such as insufficient funds. Check the payment evidence and ask the customer to contact their issuer when needed.

sections.title: Do not turn an unknown reason into a diagnosis
sections.body:
A generic issuer refusal does not tell you the customer’s balance or intent. For Visa, raw network code 05 is the network’s don’t-honor response; inspect the network and Stripe fields together. Do not label every such account fraudulent or churned.

Read the decline-code guide if your report mixes raw responses, Stripe codes, and human-readable messages.

sections.title: Inspect before attempting collection again
sections.body:
• Confirm the original invoice remains unpaid.
  • Read the latest payment failure and any retry advice.
  • Check whether card details require correction or the customer must contact the issuer.
  • Identify other active retry systems and any uncertain recent outcome.
  • Record the next action and its owner.

Do not assume that a scheduled or counted retry proves a new charge reached the network. Inspect the payment evidence for the attempt you are investigating.

sections.title: Use advice to choose the branch
sections.body:
Stripe can return advice indicating that the method should not be tried again for the transaction, that a later attempt may be appropriate, or that card data needs confirmation. Follow the actual advice rather than treating every generic refusal as an instruction to retry immediately.

Customer authentication is another distinct branch. If that is required, follow the authentication workflow. Trying another card is not permission to bypass required customer action.

sections.title: Ask for a useful customer action
sections.body:
Use neutral wording: “Your subscription payment did not complete. Please review your billing details or contact your card issuer, then use this secure billing link to resolve the invoice.” Include the genuine amount, invoice reference, and your support route.

Do not claim to know why the bank declined the card. Do not ask for a full card number, CVC, or bank statement by email. Our email templates provide reusable fields.

sections.title: When another saved card is relevant
sections.body:
If an authorized, eligible alternative exists and the invoice still needs payment, a controlled saved-card workflow may be appropriate. Rebound lets the operator start that work for selected invoices and records the outcomes. A stored card is not a recovery guarantee.

Stop on confirmed payment. If the result is unknown, investigate the original request and invoice before more collection. Use the evidence checklist to keep the result traceable.

title: Rebound vs. FlyCode: controlled collections or broader recovery?
description: Compare Rebound’s operator-started invoice recovery with FlyCode’s advertised recovery platform. Both support saved-card fallback; evaluate the workflow you need.
answer: Both Rebound and FlyCode describe recovery using alternative saved cards. Rebound focuses on an operator-started invoice run; FlyCode markets a broader automated payment recovery platform. Choose based on ownership, onboarding, and evidence—not the fallback feature alone.

sections.title: The job you are buying
sections.body:
Choose a focused operator workspace when your team wants to inspect a date-filtered invoice group and deliberately initiate its collection. Evaluate a broader platform when the requirement includes automated recovery orchestration and customer communications.

Rebound is the publisher of this comparison. This is a public-documentation comparison checked November 10, 2026, not a hands-on FlyCode benchmark. No equivalent invoice cohort was tested in both products.

sections.title: Saved-card fallback exists in both products
sections.body:
FlyCode’s Adaptive Backup Cards page describes trying another saved card after the primary fails. Its pricing page also advertises retry models, transactional emails, and reporting. These are vendor descriptions, not performance independently verified by Rebound.

Rebound’s current workflow lets an operator select a date range, review unpaid subscription invoices, and start a run. It attempts eligible distinct cards once per invoice in that run and stops when paid. It does not provide a dunning email campaign or an automatic background collection schedule.

sections.title: Questions to ask in an evaluation
sections.body:
1. Who starts collection, and can you review the invoice group first?
  2. How are existing retries coordinated?
  3. What happens after success, exhaustion, or an unknown outcome?
  4. Can a reported recovery be traced to the original invoice and request?
  5. What customer communication and onboarding are included?
  6. How are collected revenue and incremental recovery defined in the agreement?

Ask each vendor to demonstrate these questions using a safe sample workflow. A feature list alone does not establish fit.

sections.title: Pricing and evidence need a direct check
sections.body:
FlyCode advertises outcome-based pricing tied to recovery above a baseline; obtain the current quote and attribution terms directly. This page does not establish a fixed FlyCode fee or a Rebound price advantage.

Rebound’s Porter Metrics story reports $8,000 recovered in 2026 through November 9. It is customer-reported, not a controlled comparison against FlyCode or proof of incremental lift over Stripe.

sections.title: When to choose which direction
sections.body:
Evaluate Rebound when you specifically need a deliberate invoice-and-card collection workspace and can own the surrounding communication process. Evaluate FlyCode when its broader advertised recovery scope matches your requirements. Verify permissions, current terms, and operational controls with each vendor.

Inspect Rebound’s connection and controls, the product workflow, and the dunning checklist before deciding. Neither workflow can guarantee a card issuer approves a payment.

title: Rebound vs. Stunning: saved-card runs or a dunning suite?
description: Compare Rebound’s deliberate invoice recovery workflow with Stunning’s advertised emails, SMS, billing updates, and backup cards for Stripe.
answer: Rebound focuses on operator-started recovery runs across eligible saved cards. Stunning advertises a wider Stripe dunning suite including customer messages, update pages, and backup cards. Both address payment failure; they offer different operating scopes.

sections.title: Start with the missing job in your billing process
sections.body:
If the missing job is reviewing unpaid invoices and initiating collection across existing eligible cards, a focused workspace may fit. If it is persistent customer outreach and billing-update journeys, evaluate a product that supplies those features.

This comparison is published by Rebound and uses Stunning’s public feature documentation checked November 10, 2026. It is not an independent product test or a recovery-rate comparison.

sections.title: What Stunning publicly describes
sections.body:
For Stripe, Stunning advertises failed-payment emails, SMS, in-app notices, payment-update pages, reporting, and backup cards. Its backup workflow asks customers to supply a backup and describes switching to it when the main card fails. Check its current configuration and platform-specific terms directly.

That feature set is broader than Rebound’s current collection workspace. Do not assume either product’s public list describes every setting or limitation in a specific account.

sections.title: What Rebound currently does
sections.body:
Rebound loads failed subscription payments in a chosen date range and shows the original invoice, balance, saved-card count, and collection state. The operator starts a run; the tool works through eligible distinct cards once per invoice in that run, stops on success, and holds uncertain results for review.

It does not provide an email or SMS campaign, a customer card-update campaign, or an automatic background collection schedule. Our controls page explains connection and collection separately.

sections.title: Use a short buying checklist
sections.body:
• Communication: do you need the vendor to send messages, or will your existing process own them?
  • Initiation: do you need an operator to review a fixed invoice list first?
  • Saved methods: how are backup cards collected, selected, and checked?
  • Coordination: how do vendor attempts interact with Stripe and other tools?
  • Evidence: can your team explain which request paid the original invoice?
  • Commercial terms: confirm current price, scope, and cancellation terms directly.

No price ranking is asserted here. A lower headline fee is not meaningful without comparable scope.

sections.title: Keep the outcome test honest
sections.body:
Compare defined invoice cohorts over an agreed time window. Separate the vendor’s actions from payments made by customers or other processes. Do not attribute every payment after activation to the tool.

Read the attribution guide and the measurement guide. If your need spans communication and collection, map that full process before selecting a product.
